chapter_summary: Proverbs 30 contains the words of Agur son of Jakeh — a man who begins by confessing his own ignorance and unworthiness before God. From that posture of humility he asks for two things: freedom from lies and just enough provision — neither wealth nor poverty. The chapter then surveys generations who go wrong through pride, greed, and dishonour, before pivoting to four wonderful things, four wise small creatures, and four things that move with dignity. The chapter closes with a sharp warning: forcing anger always brings strife. Throughout, the fear of God, the purity of His Word, and the wisdom hidden in small things are the recurring anchors.
main_lesson: God is greater than we can fully understand. We need His Word, and we need to trust Him for just what we need — not too much, not too little.

memory_verse.kjv: Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him.
memory_verse.little_bible: Every word God says is pure and true. He protects everyone who trusts in Him.

parent_guide:
Proverbs 30 opens with a remarkable act of intellectual humility. Agur does not claim great wisdom — he confesses he is more like an animal than a wise man, and that he does not truly know the holy God. Yet this very humility is itself wisdom. Before teaching anything, Agur kneels. This is a profound model for children and parents alike: wisdom begins with knowing what we do not know, and reverencing the One who does know all things.

The prayer of verses 7–9 is one of the most theologically rich prayers in all of Scripture. Agur asks for just enough — not riches that would make him forget God, not poverty that would tempt him to steal. This is a lesson in contentment that runs directly into the New Testament (1 Timothy 6:6–8; Philippians 4:11–13). Children who grow up learning to pray for 'just enough' are forming a spiritual muscle that will serve them for life.

The small creatures in verses 24–28 are a stunning counter-cultural lesson. Ants, conies (rock hyraxes), locusts, and spiders are not powerful — but they are exceedingly wise. They plan ahead, find shelter in hard places, work together without a single boss, and reach places of honour through persistence. Help your children see that God's wisdom does not always look like strength. Faithfulness, diligence, and quiet perseverance are greater than raw power.

The chapter closes with a proverb about cause and effect that applies especially to anger: just as churning produces butter and striking the nose produces blood, so forcing wrath always produces strife. Anger management is not merely emotional — it is wise. Help your children understand that letting anger run unchecked always creates a mess, and that controlling it is one of the wisest things they can ever learn to do.
application_for_children: This week, practise the prayer of Agur: 'God, help me want just what I need — not too much, not too little.' And look for the small, wise things God made — the ant, the spider — and remember: being faithful and hardworking matters more than being the biggest or strongest.

verses.kjv: The words of Agur the son of Jakeh, even the prophecy: the man spake unto Ithiel, even unto Ithiel and Ucal,
verses.little_bible: These are the words of a man named Agur. He spoke them to his friends Ithiel and Ucal.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A man named Agur shared these wise words with his friends.
verses.meaning: Proverbs 30 opens with attribution to Agur son of Jakeh — a figure about whom little else is known. The oracle or 'prophecy' suggests these words are not merely Agur's own thoughts but a message he received and passed on. The mention of Ithiel and Ucal grounds the words in a real conversation between real people.
verses.prayer: God, help me share Your wisdom with others.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it good to pass wise words on to friends?
verses.family_discussion: How do we cultivate a culture in our family where wisdom is spoken, shared, and received — not just assumed?
verses.do_it_today: Share one wise thing you have learned with a friend or sibling today.
verses.illustration_prompt: A humble man sitting with two attentive friends under a tree, sharing words carefully, warm golden watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: Surely I am more brutish than any man, and have not the understanding of a man.
verses.little_bible: Agur said: I am not very wise at all. I do not understand things the way other people do.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Agur said he was not wise and did not understand much.
verses.meaning: Agur's opening confession is startling: he calls himself more brutish — more like an unthinking animal — than any other man, lacking the understanding a human being should have. This is not false humility but genuine recognition of his own limits before God. True wisdom begins with knowing how little we know.
verses.prayer: God, keep me humble. I need Your wisdom.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it wise to admit you do not know everything?
verses.family_discussion: How do we model intellectual humility before God and others — especially when we are used to being the most knowledgeable person in the room?
verses.do_it_today: Say to someone today: 'I don't know everything. I'm still learning.' Mean it.
verses.illustration_prompt: A small figure bowing humbly before a vast starlit sky, hand over heart, soft and reverent watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: I neither learned wisdom, nor have the knowledge of the holy.
verses.little_bible: Agur said: I have not learned wisdom on my own. I do not fully know God.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Agur admitted he had not learned wisdom or fully known God.
verses.meaning: Agur continues his honest confession: he has not attained wisdom through learning, nor does he possess knowledge of God (the Holy One) through his own effort. This is the posture that makes him teachable. Only those who know their ignorance will seek — and only those who seek will find (Proverbs 2:4–5).
verses.prayer: God, teach me what I cannot learn alone.
verses.discussion_question: Where does true wisdom about God come from?
verses.family_discussion: How do we communicate to our children that knowing God is not something they can achieve by clever thinking alone — it requires God's own revelation?
verses.do_it_today: Ask God today to teach you something from His Word that you could never figure out on your own.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child sitting with an open Bible, a gentle light from above illuminating the page, quiet and reverent, watercolour style

verses.kjv: Who hath ascended up into heaven, or descended? who hath gathered the wind in his fists? who hath bound the waters in a garment? who hath established all the ends of the earth? what is his name, and what is his son's name, if thou canst tell?
verses.little_bible: Who has gone up to heaven and come back down? Who holds the wind in His hands? Who controls the seas and set the edges of the earth in place? Only God can do these things.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Only God can hold the wind, control the sea, and set up the whole earth.
verses.meaning: Agur's rhetorical questions point unmistakably to God as the only One with power over creation. The mention of God's 'son's name' is striking — commentators throughout history have seen here a hint of the Son of God who would be revealed in Jesus Christ. No human can claim these powers; only the Creator-God and His Son.
verses.prayer: God, You alone hold the wind and sea.
verses.discussion_question: Can any person hold the wind in their hands?
verses.family_discussion: How do you help your children cultivate awe at God's power over creation — not just intellectual knowledge of it but genuine wonder?
verses.do_it_today: Go outside. Feel the wind on your face. Say: 'Only God can hold this.' Let it fill you with wonder.
verses.illustration_prompt: A vast sky with wind swirling in giant invisible hands, the ocean below, the whole earth visible at the edges, majestic watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him.
verses.little_bible: Every word God says is pure and true. He is a shield. He protects everyone who trusts in Him.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: God's words are always true. He protects those who trust Him.
verses.meaning: After establishing God's greatness in creation, Agur affirms the purity of God's Word and the protection God offers to those who trust Him. This verse is a cornerstone of biblical faith: Scripture is not contaminated by error or deception. It is refined like pure gold — and the God who speaks it personally shields those who rely on what He says.
verses.prayer: God, I trust Your Word. Be my shield today.
verses.discussion_question: Why can we always trust what God says?
verses.family_discussion: How do we cultivate in our children a deep trust in Scripture — not just as a rule book but as God's own pure, protective word spoken directly to them?
verses.do_it_today: Find one promise in the Bible. Write it down and say: 'I trust this because God said it and God is pure.'
verses.illustration_prompt: A glowing golden shield with a child safely sheltering behind it, radiant light and open Bible in the background, watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar.
verses.little_bible: Do not add your own words to what God has said. If you do, God will correct you. You will be found to be a liar.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Never add to what God says. It makes you a liar.
verses.meaning: Because God's Word is pure (v. 5), adding to it is a serious offense — it corrupts the purity of what God has said and places human words on the same level as God's. This warning resonates throughout Scripture (Deuteronomy 4:2; Revelation 22:18–19) and guards against false teaching, adding traditions to Scripture, or claiming God said things He did not.
verses.prayer: God, help me say only what You have said.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it wrong to say God said something He did not say?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children distinguish between what God has actually said in Scripture and what people claim God said — especially in an age of many voices?
verses.do_it_today: Before you tell someone 'the Bible says...' make sure you check that it actually does. Don't add to God's words.
verses.illustration_prompt: An open Bible with a clear boundary line around its words, a hand stopped from adding anything outside the line, gentle warning light, watercolour style

verses.kjv: Two things have I required of thee; deny me them not before I die:
verses.little_bible: Agur prayed: God, I am asking You for two things. Please do not say no to me while I am still alive.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Agur asked God for just two things before he died.
verses.meaning: Agur now turns to prayer — a remarkable and structured request. The framing ('before I die') gives his petition urgency and sincerity. He is not making a long wish list but two carefully chosen requests. This models the discipline of focused, prioritised prayer rather than endless general asking.
verses.prayer: God, teach me to pray for what I truly need.
verses.discussion_question: If you could ask God for just two things, what would they be?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children learn to pray purposefully — not just a scatter of requests, but thoughtful, prioritised petitions aligned with what God values?
verses.do_it_today: Write two important prayer requests and bring them to God today. Focus your whole prayer on just those two.
verses.illustration_prompt: A kneeling figure with hands raised toward a bright sky, two golden rays of light coming down in response, gentle and earnest watercolour scene

verses.kjv: Remove far from me vanity and lies: give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me:
verses.little_bible: Keep me far from empty things and from lies. Give me just enough food — not too much and not too little.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Keep me from lies, and give me just what I need — not too much or too little.
verses.meaning: Agur's two requests are: (1) deliverance from falsehood and worthless things, and (2) provision of exactly what he needs — neither wealth nor poverty. This prayer of 'just enough' is extraordinarily wise. It shows that Agur knows his own weaknesses and prays accordingly. Contentment is not passive acceptance but active trust in God's measured provision.
verses.prayer: God, keep me from lies. Give me just enough.
verses.discussion_question: Why might having too much or too little both be a problem?
verses.family_discussion: How do we teach our children contentment — the ability to be thankful for what they have, neither envying those with more nor despising those with less?
verses.do_it_today: Look at what you have today. Say: 'This is enough. Thank You, God.' Practise contentment out loud.
verses.illustration_prompt: A simple table with a modest meal, just enough bread and water, warm light, a content family giving thanks, gentle watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain.
verses.little_bible: If I have too much, I might forget You and say I do not need God. If I am too poor, I might steal and do wrong. Either way I could dishonour You.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Too much might make me forget God. Too little might make me do wrong.
verses.meaning: Agur explains the logic behind his prayer for just enough. Wealth can produce spiritual forgetfulness — the prideful declaration 'Who is the LORD?' echoes the pharaoh of Exodus and the fool of Psalm 14. Poverty can produce desperate sin — stealing and misusing God's name. Both extremes threaten his faithfulness. This is remarkable self-knowledge in service of holiness.
verses.memory_phrase: Wealth can make us forget God.
verses.prayer: God, keep me close to You in all things.
verses.discussion_question: Can having too much money make it hard to trust God?
verses.family_discussion: How do you help your children see that comfort and prosperity — good in themselves — carry the spiritual danger of self-sufficiency and forgetting God?
verses.do_it_today: Thank God for something specific today. Tell Him you do not want to forget Him, no matter what you have.
verses.illustration_prompt: Two contrasting scenes side by side: a feast table with a proud person turning away from God, and a poor person reaching for what is not theirs, gentle corrective watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: Accuse not a servant unto his master, lest he curse thee, and thou be found guilty.
verses.little_bible: Do not tell lies against a servant to their master. If you do, that servant may curse you. You will be the guilty one.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Don't get someone in trouble with lies. You will be the one who is guilty.
verses.meaning: This is a warning against bearing false witness against someone in a weaker social position. Slandering a servant to their master could result in serious harm to the servant — and judgment will fall back on the accuser. The principle is broader: stirring up trouble against the vulnerable through false accusations is a serious wrong that invites divine and social consequences.
verses.prayer: God, keep my words truthful and kind always.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it wrong to get someone in trouble with lies?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children understand that bearing false witness — even small exaggerations — against others is a serious sin, not merely a social mistake?
verses.do_it_today: If you have said something untrue about another person, go and correct it today. Tell the truth instead.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child pointing to accuse someone, but the pointing finger turning back toward themselves, moral warning in a gentle watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: There is a generation that curseth their father, and doth not bless their mother.
verses.little_bible: There are people who speak badly about their father. They say nothing good about their mother. This is deeply wrong.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Some children curse their father and say nothing kind about their mother.
verses.meaning: Verses 11–14 describe four types of wicked generations — four portraits of rebellion and evil. The first is a generation that curses the father and shows no honour to the mother. This directly violates the fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12) and is a mark of a society coming apart at its moral foundations. Dishonour of parents is not trivial — it signals the collapse of the most basic human structure God designed.
verses.prayer: God, help me honour and bless my parents.
verses.discussion_question: Why does God say we must honour our parents?
verses.family_discussion: How do we cultivate genuine honour — not just compliance or surface politeness — toward parents in our home? What does cursing or belittling parents teach children about God's order?
verses.do_it_today: Say something truly kind to or about each of your parents today. Speak a blessing over them.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child speaking harsh words while a saddened parent looks on, a contrast scene showing the right way — kind words and a warm hug, watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: There is a generation that are pure in their own eyes, and yet is not washed from their filthiness.
verses.little_bible: Some people think they are clean and good inside. But they have never been truly washed from their sin. They are fooling themselves.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Some people think they are good, but they are still dirty with sin inside.
verses.meaning: The second wicked generation is one of self-righteousness. They believe themselves to be morally clean while remaining unwashed from genuine moral filth. This is a portrait of self-deception — the spiritual blindness that prevents people from seeing their own need for cleansing. Only God can truly cleanse from sin, and only those who know they are dirty will seek that cleansing (1 John 1:8–9).
verses.prayer: God, wash me clean. I cannot clean myself.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it dangerous to think you are good when you are not?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children develop a biblically honest view of themselves — neither crushing self-worth nor producing the dangerous self-righteousness described here?
verses.do_it_today: Ask God to show you one thing in your heart that needs to be cleaned. Then ask Him to clean it.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child looking in a mirror thinking they are spotless, but the mirror shows the truth — smudges of dirt visible, gentle and convicting watercolour scene

verses.kjv: There is a generation, O how lofty are their eyes! and their eyelids are lifted up.
verses.little_bible: Some people walk around looking down on everyone else. Their eyes are lifted high with pride. They think they are better than others.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Some people are very proud and look down on everyone else.
verses.meaning: The third wicked generation is characterised by pride — specifically the pride of contempt. 'Lofty eyes' and 'lifted eyelids' are ancient images of disdain, looking down at others as beneath oneself. God consistently opposes this posture (Proverbs 6:17; Isaiah 2:11–12). Pride that demeans others is not merely arrogance — it is a declaration of war against the order God has established.
verses.prayer: God, keep my heart humble and my eyes kind.
verses.discussion_question: What does it look like when someone acts like they are better than everyone?
verses.family_discussion: How do we address pride in ourselves and our children — especially the subtle kind that does not declare itself loudly but quietly looks down on those it considers inferior?
verses.do_it_today: Find one person you have looked down on and treat them with extra kindness and respect today.
verses.illustration_prompt: A proud figure with eyes lifted high, looking over others below, a contrast image of a humble child kneeling to help another, watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: There is a generation, whose teeth are as swords, and their jaw teeth as knives, to devour the poor from off the earth, and the needy from among men.
verses.little_bible: Some people use their words like swords and knives. They attack the poor. They destroy those who have nothing and need help.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Some people use cruel words to hurt and devour those who are poor and helpless.
verses.meaning: The fourth wicked generation is predatory — they use their words and power to consume the poor and needy. The image of teeth as swords is vivid: words and social power wielded like weapons against the most vulnerable. This echoes the prophetic condemnations throughout the Old Testament (Isaiah 10:1–2; Amos 5:11–12). Cruelty toward the poor is not a political issue in Scripture — it is a moral catastrophe.
verses.prayer: God, help me protect people who need help.
verses.discussion_question: How do we treat people who have less than us?
verses.family_discussion: How do we cultivate in our children a genuine compassion for the poor — one rooted not in pity but in the understanding that attacking the vulnerable is among the gravest sins Scripture describes?
verses.do_it_today: Find one way to help someone who needs it today — give something, share something, or speak up for someone being treated badly.
verses.illustration_prompt: Sharp sword-like teeth contrasted with gentle hands reaching down to help a small vulnerable figure, dramatic yet redemptive watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: The horseleach hath two daughters, crying, Give, give. There are three things that are never satisfied, yea, four things say not, It is enough:
verses.little_bible: A leech has two daughters that always cry, 'Give! Give!' There are four things that are never full. They always want more.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Some things are never satisfied — they always want more and more.
verses.meaning: The horseleach (a large bloodsucking leech) is used as an image of insatiable craving. Its two daughters — named 'Give! Give!' — represent the voice of every appetite that can never be filled. Verses 15–16 then list four things that share this quality of never being satisfied. The lesson is about the danger of uncontrolled desire: some appetites, left unchecked, never stop.
verses.prayer: God, free me from greed. Help me be thankful.
verses.discussion_question: What happens when someone always wants more and is never happy?
verses.family_discussion: How do we identify the 'Give! Give!' voices in our own lives and our children's lives — whether for food, screens, toys, or approval — and address them honestly?
verses.do_it_today: Think of something you always seem to want more of. Choose to be grateful for what you already have instead.
verses.illustration_prompt: A leech-like creature with an ever-open mouth and two tiny daughters crying 'Give! Give!', around them four unsatisfied things, curious and cautionary watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: The grave; and the barren womb; the earth that is not filled with water; and the fire that saith not, It is enough.
verses.little_bible: The grave never has enough people. A woman who cannot have children always longs for a child. Dry ground is always thirsty for rain. Fire always wants more to burn.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: The grave, dry ground, and fire are never full — they always want more.
verses.meaning: The four unsatisfied things are: death (the grave always receives more), barrenness (an unfulfilled longing), parched earth (endless thirst for water), and fire (which always consumes more). These are powerful natural images of insatiable appetite. Together they warn that certain hungers — especially those rooted in death and destruction — can never be satisfied by giving them more. The only solution is transformation, not indulgence.
verses.prayer: God, satisfy my heart. You are enough for me.
verses.discussion_question: What is the only thing that can truly satisfy the deepest hunger in your heart?
verses.family_discussion: How do we point our children to God as the only One whose presence truly satisfies — and help them recognise when they are trying to fill spiritual emptiness with things that cannot fill it?
verses.do_it_today: Tell God what your heart is most hungry for. Ask Him to be enough for you.
verses.illustration_prompt: Four panels: an open grave, a longing woman, cracked dry earth, and a hungry fire — each with an empty outstretched hand, solemn and beautiful watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: The eye that mocketh at his father, and despiseth to obey his mother, the ravens of the valley shall pick it out, and the young eagles shall eat it.
verses.little_bible: If you mock your father and refuse to obey your mother, it will end very badly for you. God does not ignore this sin. Dishonour brings serious consequences.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Mocking your parents and refusing to obey brings very serious consequences.
verses.meaning: The graphic imagery (ravens picking out the mocking eye) is a poetic picture of divine judgment on those who dishonour their parents. The eye that looks with contempt at a father and the heart that refuses a mother's instruction will face the consequences of that contempt. This is not cruelty — it is the solemn declaration that the parent-child relationship is sacred and that God defends it.
verses.prayer: God, help me never mock or despise my parents.
verses.discussion_question: What does it mean to mock or despise your parents?
verses.family_discussion: How do you respond when children roll their eyes, use sarcastic tones, or subtly undermine parental authority? How do we name this clearly as the serious sin the Bible calls it?
verses.do_it_today: Ask yourself honestly: do I sometimes roll my eyes, speak sarcastically, or refuse to obey my parents? Choose to change that today.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child looking with contempt at a parent, ravens circling in the dark sky above as a warning, solemn and dramatic watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: There be three things which are too wonderful for me, yea, four which I know not:
verses.little_bible: Agur said: There are three things that fill me with wonder. In fact, four things I cannot fully understand.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Agur said four things filled him with wonder and awe.
verses.meaning: The tone shifts from warning to wonder. Agur now turns to marvellous things — things that fill him with awe because he cannot fully understand them. This models the posture of a wise person: they are not only alert to what is wrong in the world, but genuinely amazed by what is mysterious and beautiful. Wonder is itself a spiritual virtue.
verses.prayer: God, fill my heart with wonder at Your world.
verses.discussion_question: What is something in God's world that fills you with wonder?
verses.family_discussion: How do we nurture a sense of reverent wonder in our children — the ability to pause, to observe, and to be genuinely amazed — in an age that moves so fast?
verses.do_it_today: Find one thing in nature today that you cannot fully explain or understand. Sit with that wonder for a moment.
verses.illustration_prompt: A curious wide-eyed child looking up at something vast and mysterious — a night sky, an eagle soaring — filled with wonder, gentle watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: The way of an eagle in the air; the way of a serpent upon a rock; the way of a ship in the midst of the sea; and the way of a man with a maid.
verses.little_bible: How does an eagle fly through the air with no tracks? How does a snake glide over rock? How does a ship sail across the deep sea? These are marvellous things.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: An eagle in the sky, a snake on a rock, a ship at sea — all wonderful and mysterious.
verses.meaning: The four wonders are: the eagle's flight (effortless mastery of the air), the snake's movement over rock (silent, trackless motion), the ship's path through the sea (leaving no trace on the deep), and the way of a man with a maiden (the mystery of love and attraction between two people). All four leave no trace and cannot be fully explained — they are marvels of created nature.
verses.memory_phrase: God's creation fills us with awe.
verses.prayer: God, Your creation is full of wonderful mystery.
verses.discussion_question: What is the most amazing thing you have ever seen in nature?
verses.family_discussion: How do you use the marvels of creation — eagles, oceans, animals — as regular invitations for your children to encounter the greatness of the Creator?
verses.do_it_today: Watch a bird fly today. Really watch. Think: God made that eagle soar. It fills Him with joy.
verses.illustration_prompt: Four beautiful wonder scenes side by side: eagle soaring, snake gliding on rock, ship on vast sea, two figures walking together at sunset, wonder-filled watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: Such is the way of an adulterous woman; she eateth, and wipeth her mouth, and saith, I have done no wickedness.
verses.little_bible: A woman who does wrong in marriage acts like nothing happened. She wipes her mouth and says she did no wrong. She does not feel sorry for her sin.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Some people do wrong and feel no shame or sorry at all.
verses.meaning: This verse contrasts with the wonders of v. 19. The adulterous woman is not wonderful — she is brazenly unrepentant. She sins, wipes her mouth (as if she has merely eaten a meal), and declares her innocence. This is a portrait of a seared conscience — sin committed with such ease and lack of remorse that the person genuinely feels nothing. It is a warning about where unrepentant sin leads: to moral numbness.
verses.prayer: God, keep my conscience soft. Help me feel sorry for sin.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it dangerous to do wrong and feel nothing about it?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children maintain a tender conscience — one that feels the weight of doing wrong — rather than the hardened conscience that sin repeated without repentance produces?
verses.do_it_today: When you do something wrong today, stop and say sorry to God right away. Don't wipe your mouth and pretend nothing happened.
verses.illustration_prompt: A figure wiping her mouth with a casual expression, contrast with a broken mirror reflecting the reality of what has been done, serious yet gentle watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: For three things the earth is disquieted, and for four which it cannot bear:
verses.little_bible: Three things shake the whole earth. Four things the earth simply cannot handle. These are things that turn everything upside down.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Some things shake and disturb the whole world when they happen.
verses.meaning: Agur now introduces another numerical pattern — this time of things that disturb the natural order so profoundly that the whole earth is unsettled. These four scenarios (vv. 22–23) involve people in the wrong place with the wrong character. When order is overthrown by those unfit for their position, the consequences ripple everywhere.
verses.prayer: God, help me be right where You put me.
verses.discussion_question: What happens when the wrong kind of person is in charge?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children understand the importance of character matching position — that authority, responsibility, and privilege come with the need for wisdom and integrity?
verses.do_it_today: Think about a responsibility you have. Ask God to give you the character to handle it well.
verses.illustration_prompt: The earth shaking and trembling under heavy pressure from above, things out of place and topsy-turvy, illustrative watercolour scene with a sense of disorder

verses.kjv: For a servant when he reigneth; and a fool when he is filled with meat;
verses.little_bible: The earth shakes when a servant suddenly becomes king. It also shakes when a foolish person becomes satisfied and proud.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: When a fool becomes rich and proud, things go wrong for everyone.
verses.meaning: Two of the four disturbing scenarios: a servant who gains power without the character to wield it, and a fool who is well-fed and comfortable. Neither has developed the inner life or wisdom that their new position demands. Prosperity given to a fool does not make them wise — it makes them worse. Power without character corrupts those around the leader.
verses.prayer: God, grow my character before You give me more.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it dangerous to give too much power to a foolish person?
verses.family_discussion: How do you teach your children that responsibility must be earned through character, not simply given? How do you prepare them for greater authority by developing wisdom first?
verses.do_it_today: Ask a parent: 'What character quality do you think I need to grow in before I get more responsibility?' Listen carefully.
verses.illustration_prompt: A servant suddenly seated on a throne looking confused and dangerous, contrast with a wise leader who is calm and steady, cautionary watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: For an odious woman when she is married; and an handmaid that is heir to her mistress.
verses.little_bible: The earth shakes when a hateful woman gets married. It also shakes when a servant girl takes the place of her mistress. These things upset the right order of life.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: When someone cruel or out of place gets power, everything is disturbed.
verses.meaning: The final two disturbing scenarios: a hateful or odious woman whose marriage gives her new power she uses poorly, and a servant girl who supplants her mistress. Both involve the disruption of order through the wrong kind of person arriving in a position they are not equipped for morally or relationally. The emphasis is not on gender roles but on character fitness — a theme running through all four scenarios.
verses.prayer: God, make my character strong and good inside.
verses.discussion_question: Why does the kind of person you are matter more than the position you have?
verses.family_discussion: How do we communicate to our children that who they are matters infinitely more than what position or title they hold? How do we model character-first thinking in our family decisions?
verses.do_it_today: Ask yourself: am I the kind of person who would handle more responsibility well? What do you need God to grow in you?
verses.illustration_prompt: A figure stepping into a place they are not prepared for, surrounding people unsettled, contrast with a humble person growing quietly into their role, watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: There be four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise:
verses.little_bible: There are four small creatures on the earth. They are tiny and not powerful. But they are extremely wise. Pay attention to them.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Four tiny creatures are not strong, but they are very, very wise.
verses.meaning: Agur now turns from the disturbing to the instructive. Four small creatures — ants, conies, locusts, spiders — are 'exceeding wise.' The word for wisdom here implies practical skill and insight. Size and strength are not the measures of wisdom. These small things accomplish extraordinary things through diligence, planning, cooperation, and persistence. Wisdom is available to the small.
verses.prayer: God, help me be wise even when I feel small.
verses.discussion_question: What is a small creature that does something amazing?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children see that wisdom is not about age, size, or power — and that God has designed even the tiniest creatures to teach us profound lessons about how to live?
verses.do_it_today: Watch a small creature today — an ant, a spider, a bird. Ask God: what is this tiny thing teaching me about wisdom?
verses.illustration_prompt: Four tiny creatures — ant, rock hyrax, locust, spider — each shown in their remarkable environment, small but purposeful and glowing with subtle wisdom, watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: The ants are a people not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer;
verses.little_bible: Ants are not strong at all. But they work hard in summer. They gather food and store it for winter. That is wise planning ahead.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Ants are tiny, but they plan ahead and work hard in summer.
verses.meaning: The ant appears in Proverbs 6:6–8 as well — always as an example of diligence and foresight. Ants have no strength, no leader commanding them, and yet they know what season it is and what to do. They plan ahead. This is a rebuke to laziness and procrastination, and a commendation of the virtue of preparation.
verses.prayer: God, help me work hard and plan wisely.
verses.discussion_question: Why is it wise to get ready before winter or hard times come?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children develop the discipline of preparation — doing the hard work now before the need becomes urgent? How do we model this in our own lives?
verses.do_it_today: Do one task today that you have been putting off. Like the ant, prepare before you need to.
verses.illustration_prompt: Tiny ants carrying food in a long industrious line under a bright summer sun, preparing for the cold season ahead, warm energetic watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks;
verses.little_bible: Conies are small and weak animals. But they build their homes in the rocks. The rocks keep them safe. They know where to go for protection.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Conies are small and weak, but they find safety in the rocks.
verses.meaning: The cony (rock hyrax) is small and physically defenceless — yet it is wise enough to shelter in the rocks where predators cannot easily reach it. Its wisdom is not strength but discernment: it knows where safety is and goes there. For God's people, the rock of safety is God Himself (Psalm 18:2, 31:3). Knowing where to run for safety is itself a form of wisdom.
verses.prayer: God, You are my rock. I run to You.
verses.discussion_question: Where do you run when you are scared or in danger?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children's first instinct in trouble be to run to God — to prayer, to His Word — rather than to anxiety, self-reliance, or other people?
verses.do_it_today: When you feel scared today, say out loud: 'God, You are my rock. I trust You.' Run to Him in prayer.
verses.illustration_prompt: A small furry cony nestled safely between massive protective rocks, tiny but secure and peaceful, warm and sheltering watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: The locusts have no king, yet go they forth all of them by bands;
verses.little_bible: Locusts have no king or leader over them. But they all move together as one. They work as a team without being told to.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Locusts have no king, but they all work together as one.
verses.meaning: Locusts are one of the most formidable forces in nature — yet they have no central command structure. Their remarkable collective movement is built into them by God. The lesson here is about unity, cooperation, and shared purpose. When people work together in the right direction, they accomplish extraordinary things — even without a single human leader issuing commands.
verses.prayer: God, help me work well with others for You.
verses.discussion_question: What can a team do that one person alone cannot?
verses.family_discussion: How do we build a culture of cooperation in our family — where each person contributes to a shared goal without needing to be pushed or commanded every step?
verses.do_it_today: Find a way to help your family or a group today without being asked. Be like the locusts — work together.
verses.illustration_prompt: A vast coordinated swarm of locusts moving in perfect unity across a field, no single leader visible, yet completely organised, dramatic and instructive watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: The spider taketh hold with her hands, and is in kings' palaces.
verses.little_bible: A spider grabs on with its small hands and climbs. It gets all the way into the palace of a king. Persistence takes you to great places.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A tiny spider climbs with persistence and reaches a king's palace.
verses.meaning: The spider (or lizard, in some translations) reaches royal palaces not through strength or status but through grip — through persistent holding on. It cannot be kept out by walls or guards because it simply keeps climbing. This is a powerful image of perseverance: small, weak things that keep reaching, keep holding, keep going — can end up in the highest places.
verses.prayer: God, help me not give up. Help me keep going.
verses.discussion_question: What should you do when something is hard and you want to give up?
verses.family_discussion: How do we cultivate perseverance in our children — the ability to keep holding on when something is difficult — especially in spiritual disciplines like prayer, Bible reading, and obedience?
verses.do_it_today: Pick one thing you have been tempted to give up on. Keep going today. Be like the spider — hold on.
verses.illustration_prompt: A tiny spider climbing the great stone wall of a magnificent palace, small and determined, reaching the high window, perseverance illustrated in warm watercolour

verses.kjv: There be three things which go well, yea, four are comely in going:
verses.little_bible: Three things move in a beautiful way. Four things are graceful and strong when they walk or move. These are things that look right.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Some creatures move with beauty and grace and strength.
verses.meaning: Agur now turns from wise small creatures to things of impressive bearing — creatures and people that move with dignity, authority, and grace. This is an appreciation of God-given excellence: not arrogance, but the proper confidence of something or someone fully inhabiting what they were made to be. There is a rightness and beauty to things functioning in their God-designed purpose.
verses.prayer: God, help me live well the life You made me for.
verses.discussion_question: What is a creature that moves in a way that fills you with wonder?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children understand that God designed each of them for a purpose — and that living fully in that purpose has a particular grace and beauty that honours God?
verses.do_it_today: Think about one thing you do really well. Thank God for making you that way. Use it today for His glory.
verses.illustration_prompt: Four majestic beings moving with grace and dignity — a lion, a rooster, a goat, a king — each in their element, stately and beautiful watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: A lion which is strongest among beasts, and turneth not away for any;
verses.little_bible: The lion is the strongest of all animals. It does not run from anything or anyone. It walks with courage and great strength.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: The lion is the strongest beast and fears nothing at all.
verses.meaning: The lion's strength and fearlessness make it the first of the four comely things. It does not retreat. It does not look over its shoulder nervously. It walks with the confident authority of the apex creature. For God's people, this is a picture of the righteous who 'are bold as a lion' (Proverbs 28:1) — those who walk in integrity need not be afraid.
verses.prayer: God, give me lion-courage to do what is right.
verses.discussion_question: What does it look like to walk with courage when you know you are doing right?
verses.family_discussion: How do you cultivate holy boldness in your children — the kind that is not arrogance but the confidence of those who walk uprightly before God and therefore have nothing to hide?
verses.do_it_today: Do one thing today that you have been afraid to do because of what others might think. Walk like a lion.
verses.illustration_prompt: A magnificent lion walking forward without hesitation, head held high, the jungle parting before it, bold and serene, beautiful watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: A greyhound; an he goat also; and a king, against whom there is no rising up.
verses.little_bible: A greyhound runs with speed and power. A male goat leads the herd with confidence. A king whom no one can challenge moves with great authority. These go well.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: A greyhound, a goat, and a strong king all move with grace and power.
verses.meaning: The other three comely things are the greyhound (possibly a war horse or fighting cock, depending on translation), the he-goat leading his flock, and a king who is unchallenged and secure. What connects them is the quality of being fully what they were made to be — authority, grace, and strength in their proper expression. The king here is not tyrannical but secure, moving without the nervous aggression of those who fear uprising.
verses.prayer: God, help me lead well in the places You give me.
verses.discussion_question: What makes a leader truly strong and worth following?
verses.family_discussion: What does grace-filled, secure leadership look like in a parent? How do we lead our families without the anxiety or aggression that comes from insecurity?
verses.do_it_today: Lead someone today — a younger sibling, a friend — with patience and confidence, not pushing or forcing. Lead like a shepherd.
verses.illustration_prompt: A greyhound in full graceful stride, a he-goat leading his flock confidently, a serene king walking among his people — all three moving with dignity, vibrant watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: If thou hast done foolishly in lifting up thyself, or if thou hast thought evil, lay thine hand upon thy mouth.
verses.little_bible: If you have acted in pride or thought evil thoughts, stop now. Put your hand over your mouth. Do not say another word. Be still.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: If you have been proud or thought evil, stop and be quiet right now.
verses.meaning: This verse is a direct and urgent call to self-arrest — to stop the progression from proud thought to evil word to destructive action. Placing the hand over the mouth is an ancient gesture of silence, restraint, and humility (see Job 40:4). The wise person, when they recognise their own foolishness in progress, stops immediately. This is the first act of repentance: ceasing.
verses.prayer: God, help me stop when I am going the wrong way.
verses.discussion_question: What should you do the moment you realise you are being proud or thinking wrong thoughts?
verses.family_discussion: How do we help our children develop the habit of self-stopping — the ability to recognise mid-course that they are heading the wrong direction and cease, before words or actions make things worse?
verses.do_it_today: The next time you want to say something proud or unkind, put your hand over your mouth for two seconds. Then choose a better word or none at all.
verses.illustration_prompt: A child mid-sentence, catching themselves, gently placing their own hand over their mouth in a moment of honest self-restraint, peaceful resolution, watercolour illustration

verses.kjv: Surely the churning of milk bringeth forth butter, and the wringing of the nose bringeth forth blood: so the forcing of wrath bringeth forth strife.
verses.little_bible: When you churn milk, butter comes out. When you press a nose hard, blood comes out. When you keep pushing anger, fighting always comes out. Anger forced always leads to strife.
verses.little_reader_adaptation: Pushing anger always produces a fight. It works every single time.
verses.meaning: The chapter closes with a cause-and-effect proverb that is inescapable in its logic. Churning produces butter — that is the natural result. Striking the nose produces blood — that is the natural result. Forcing wrath (pressing, intensifying, or provoking anger) produces strife — that is the natural result, every time, without exception. Anger is not neutral. If you keep pushing it, conflict is not a possibility — it is a certainty.
verses.prayer: God, help me not force anger. Give me peace.
verses.discussion_question: What always happens when people keep pushing and forcing their anger?
verses.family_discussion: How do we teach our children the law of cause and effect in their emotions — that some things, if pushed, always produce the same outcome? How do we stop the churn before it begins?
verses.do_it_today: The next time you feel angry, stop before you push it further. Breathe. Say: 'Forcing this will only make a fight.' Choose peace.
verses.illustration_prompt: Three side-by-side images: cream being churned into butter, a nose pressed bringing a drop of blood, two people in strife from forced anger — a clear natural law illustrated in watercolour
